## 1. NARRATIVE ARC

The story management tells shifted decisively over these five quarters — from "survival and repositioning" to "we are becoming an AI-native company." EPAM is a digital-engineering and custom-software-development outsourcer: it builds software for large enterprises using globally distributed engineering talent (historically anchored in Central and Eastern Europe, now spread across India, Latin America, and Western/Central Asia).

Early in 2025 (Q1 call, May), the dominant theme was cautious relief. After a bruising 2022–2024 — when the war in Ukraine forced a scramble to diversify its delivery base away from Eastern Europe and organic growth went negative — management framed 2025 as "a year of transition" and repeatedly hedged the second half: "reality of H2 is very difficult to predict." The same call carried a founder-CEO succession: Arkadiy Dobkin, after 32 years, handed the reins to Balazs Fejes ("FB"), effective September 1, 2025.

By Q3 (November) and Q4 (February 2026), the narrative had flipped to offense. The refrain became "we are entering an age of building" and EPAM as "the world's leading AI-native transformation company." The company introduced a new, quantified growth pillar — "pure AI-native revenue" — that did not exist in the early-2025 vocabulary: more than $105M in Q4 alone, and a stated goal to scale it beyond $600M in 2026. The old defensive language ("prudent," "very careful," "difficult to predict") gave way to "very, very bullish" (FB, Q4).

What was quietly dropped: the hand-wringing about H2 visibility, and any dwelling on the Eastern-Europe/Ukraine delivery risk that dominated the prior narrative — by Q2 management declared its geographic repositioning essentially complete ("we're in good shape... between all major hubs").

## 2. CLAIMS vs FINANCIALS (forensic)

Management's words are the hypothesis; the numbers are the evidence. Here is where they agree and diverge.

| Management claim | The financial evidence | Verdict |
|---|---|---|
| "Return to double-digit revenue growth," "strongest organic constant-currency growth in the industry" | Revenue did reaccelerate: +15.4% year-over-year in the latest fiscal year, and 2025 revenue of $5.46B vs $4.73B in 2024. But the 3-year revenue compound growth is only +4.2% — the double-digit print is off a depressed base and heavily aided by two acquisitions (First Derivative, NEORIS) and a weaker dollar. | **Richer than the trend** — the headline flatters a low-single-digit underlying run-rate. Q4 organic growth was only +5.6%, and the FY2026 organic guide is just 3–6%. |

This is the strongest pillar of the value case. |

**Rising** — measurably so, quarter by quarter.

- **Q1 2025 (May):** hedged and defensive. "We balancing the good message with a difficult, very difficult environment." Dobkin repeatedly refused to project H2.
- **Q2 2025 (Aug):** more confident. "Organic growth accelerated from the low single digits to the mid-single digits... all six verticals growing."
- **Q3 2025 (Nov, FB's first call):** distinctly upbeat. FB opened with espresso jokes and "positive news to share... fourth consecutive quarter of positive year-over-year organic constant-currency growth" of 7.1%.
- **Q4 2025 (Feb 2026):** the most bullish of all — but notably, this is where the *market* stopped believing. FB called the AI-eats-software debate "a tremendous opportunity" and declared himself "very, very bullish."

The tell: confidence rose steadily even as the reported earnings line fell. Management got more specific and more offensive with its AI language precisely as the profit trajectory deteriorated — a gap the director should weigh.

**High on the metric they choose to guide; Medium on what actually matters to owners.** EPAM beat consensus 7 of the last 7 quarters — a perfect near-term beat rate — and each of the five calls opened with "results came in better than expected." Management spent all of 2025 guiding to a recovery, and the recovery in revenue was real — yet it did not translate into earnings, and the very next guide (FY2026, issued February 2026) cut organic growth back to 3–6% and, on the May 2026 Q1 call, was narrowed again to 4–6.5% on "North American client decision delays." The questions recurred, and management's answers thinned each time:

- **Bill-rate / pricing under AI** (Bryan Keane, Citi, Q4): "any AI pressure... on the pricing that gets passed on?" The CFO's answer leaned on structure — "we don't have BPO, we don't have application maintenance" — rather than data. This is the load-bearing bear question, and it was deflected with reassurance, not evidence.
- **Does AI reduce the need to hire?** (Paul Obrecht for Darrin Peller, Q3): FB asserted "demand increase will outstrip any efficiency gains." An assertion, not a demonstration — and the falling net margin cuts the other way.
- **Build-vs-buy and GenAI revenue size** (Antonio Jaramillo for James Faucette, Q3): management could not cleanly quantify GenAI revenue, calling it "a little bit hard for me to tell exactly what you're looking for."
- **Second-half visibility** (Puneet Jain, Q1; Jim Schneider, Q1): repeatedly non-answered — "predicting Q3, Q4 better than we predicted so far is difficult."

The through-line: analysts kept probing whether AI compresses the billable-hour model, and management kept answering with conviction rather than numbers.

🔴 Revenue +15% while earnings per share -14% in the same year — growth is not converting to profit.
🔴 Gross margin explicitly contracting; net margin at 6.9%, well below peer Accenture's ~11%.
🔴 The single biggest analyst worry (AI compressing bill rates in a labor-arbitrage model) is met with reassurance, not disclosure.
🔴 FY2026 organic guide cut twice (to 3–6%, then narrowed to 4–6.5%) on "North American client decision delays" — the demand softness management spent 2025 denying is showing up.
🔴 Founder-CEO stepped back after 32 years — a real transition risk, however well-telegraphed.

🟢 Fortress balance sheet: ~$749M net cash, strong free cash flow ($544M trailing-twelve-month, +16% year-over-year), and a real $1B buyback authorization being actively used.
🟢 Four consecutive quarters of positive organic growth after the 2022–2024 slump — the core business did stabilize.
🟢 Pure AI-native revenue is a genuine, growing line ($105M+ in Q4, targeted past $600M in 2026) and credible external validation (Microsoft/AWS/Google partner-of-year awards, top-5 SWE-bench, Gartner leader, an Anthropic partnership).
🟢 Perfect 7/7 quarterly beat rate — management does not over-promise the near quarter.

## 7. HIDDEN SIGNALS

- **A vocabulary swap that reveals the strategy shift:** "cost takeout" and "supplier consolidation" (early 2025, defensive) gave way to "age of building," "client zero," and "AI-native transformation company" (late 2025, offensive). EPAM is repositioning from a cost-arbitrage vendor to a premium AI-transformation partner — a necessary pivot, but an unproven one at the margin line.
- **The new CEO's framing of the existential risk is the most important signal.** Asked directly about "AI eating software," FB reframed it as build-versus-buy tilting toward *build*: "There is no limit to how much software people want to build... we are a builder... we are not input limited." This is the entire bull case in one sentence — and it is a thesis, not yet a proven fact in the numbers.
- **Commercial-model drift:** management flagged fixed-fee revenue rising (toward ~20%+ of mix) and "subscription models" on EPAM's own platforms (DIAL, AI/RUN). A shift away from pure time-and-materials could either protect margins (outcome-based pricing) or expose them (fixed-fee risk if AI productivity is passed to clients).
- **Capital allocation turned decisively toward buybacks** as the stock fell — "with the share price where it is today, you'll continue to see us reasonably active... particularly in the first half of 2026." Management is voting with the balance sheet at these prices.

## 8. CAPITAL-ALLOCATION VERDICT (for the director)

**Trajectory: PIVOTING.** This is not a clean strengthening story (earnings are falling) nor a clean deterioration (the core stabilized, cash is strong, growth reaccelerated at the top line). It is a business mid-pivot: from a labor-arbitrage engineering shop into an AI-native transformation partner, self-funding an aggressive buyback while the market violently re-rates the multiple down.

**The single most important thing to weigh before sizing:** whether AI is a tailwind or a solvent for EPAM's economics. The bull (management's) case is that AI multiplies the amount of software enterprises want built, and EPAM — a premium builder, not a commodity maintainer — captures that. The bear case is written in this year's own numbers: revenue up 15%, earnings per share down 14%, gross margin contracting, in a business that fundamentally bills for human hours. If AI decouples revenue from headcount, a low multiple on a shrinking-margin base is a value trap, not a bargain.

**Moat:** intangible/reputational (engineering-quality brand, deep client relationships, switching costs on complex programs) — but **eroding**. Return on invested capital of ~12.5% is respectable yet the margin structure is compressing and net margin (6.9%) already trails best-in-class peers. A high-but-falling return profile is an eroding moat, not a wide one.

**Secular threat:** the labor-arbitrage-deflation / AI-displacement force is **material** — not yet clearly terminal (EPAM's premium-build positioning and no-BPO/no-managed-services mix genuinely insulate it more than a commodity staff-augmentation shop), but it is the live driver of both the earnings decline and the multiple collapse. The cheapness is part fear-print, part justified by real earnings-quality erosion. This is a special-situation buyback-and-net-cash value case sitting on top of an unresolved structural question, not a clean mispricing.

## 1. NARRATIVE ARC

The story management tells shifted decisively over these five quarters — from "survival and repositioning" to "we are becoming an AI-native company." EPAM is a digital-engineering and custom-software-development outsourcer: it builds software for large enterprises using globally distributed engineering talent (historically anchored in Central and Eastern Europe, now spread across India, Latin America, and Western/Central Asia).

Early in 2025 (Q1 call, May), the dominant theme was cautious relief. After a bruising 2022–2024 — when the war in Ukraine forced a scramble to diversify its delivery base away from Eastern Europe and organic growth went negative — management framed 2025 as "a year of transition" and repeatedly hedged the second half: "reality of H2 is very difficult to predict." The same call carried a founder-CEO succession: Arkadiy Dobkin, after 32 years, handed the reins to Balazs Fejes ("FB"), effective September 1, 2025.

By Q3 (November) and Q4 (February 2026), the narrative had flipped to offense. The refrain became "we are entering an age of building" and EPAM as "the world's leading AI-native transformation company." The company introduced a new, quantified growth pillar — "pure AI-native revenue" — that did not exist in the early-2025 vocabulary: more than $105M in Q4 alone, and a stated goal to scale it beyond $600M in 2026. The old defensive language ("prudent," "very careful," "difficult to predict") gave way to "very, very bullish" (FB, Q4).

Management's words are the hypothesis; the numbers are the evidence. Here is where they agree and diverge.

Q4 organic growth was only +5.6%, and the FY2026 organic guide is just 3–6%. |

Net margin is 6.9% — thin, and it *fell*: net income dropped from $455M (2024) to $378M (2025) even as revenue rose. Earnings per share fell from $7.84 to $6.72, a -14.3% year-over-year decline. | **Poorer than the story** — this is the central tension. Revenue grew 15% while profit *shrank*.
